name: Kyoto Gyoen National Garden
description: A large public park surrounding Kyoto Imperial Palace, covering approximately 1.3 km north–south and 700 m east–west. The grounds were formerly occupied by the residences of imperial family members and court nobles, many of which were demolished following the Meiji Restoration and the transfer of the capital to Tokyo. Today the park contains extensive lawns, wooded paths, plum and cherry groves, historic gates and the sites of former aristocratic residences. Notable features include the Kan-in-no-miya Residence exhibition centre, the Edo-period Shūsui-tei teahouse and the remains of the Konoe family residence.

description: Higashi Honganji was established in 1602 by the Shogun Tokugawa Ieyasu when he split the Shin sect in two (Nishi Honganji being the other) in order to diminish its power. Today it is the headquarters of the Ōtani branch of Jōdo Shin-shū. The Founder’s Hall (Goei-dō) is said to be the second-largest wooden structure in Japan. With a capacity for 5,000 people, it's majestic. Check out the massive coil of hair rope, donated by a group of female devotees and used to haul the massive timbers for the reconstruction of the temple in the 1880s.

There are two tourist information centers in the building on the 2nd and 9th floors. description: A museum devoted to the archaeology and early history of Kyoto, displaying around 1,000 artefacts recovered from excavations across the city. The collection covers the Palaeolithic period through the Jōmon, Yayoi, Kofun, Heian and later periods, illustrating the development of settlement and urban life before and after Kyoto became Japan's capital in 794. Exhibits include prehistoric pottery, stone tools, roof tiles, wooden implements, trade goods from China and Korea, and finds from the Heian Palace, including objects from the former Toyotomi Hall (Hōrakuden).

name: National Diet Building
description: Housing Japan's bicameral legislature, it was built in the 1920s. The most recognizable symbol of the Japanese government, it was built from Japanese building materials, features a pyramidal roof and is surrounded with green areas. The nearby free Kensei Kinenkan (between the Diet and the water) has a nice view on it, and tons of political artefacts to satisfy those interested in Japanese politics. English tours are available on weekdays by reservation only, but the tour focuses almost exclusively on the architecture of the Diet Building such as the origin of building materials or the dimensions of rooms, with little consideration for political procedure or historicity.

name: Jakarta History Museum
description: The building was a city hall (Stadhuis) until 1710, and then an underground prison, and used as the provincial office before restored into its use today as Jakarta's History Museum in 1974. Start from the right entrance, the first room you'll encounter is the transportation mode Jakarta used, including carts. Next, the chronology begins with writing on the stones that tell the growth of the area from as early as the 5th century, then the Portuguese and the Dutch. The backyard has the famous Jagur cannon. Other highlights include the fusion of cultures from both in and out of Indonesia and the assimilation that shapes the local Betawi culture. The basement used to be a dark prison of torture.

It displays around 90 works from a collection totalling 800 modern Indonesian and contemporary artworks from around the world including 'Infinity Mirrored Room' by Japanese artist Yayoi Kusama. The museum is not frightened to exhibit artists who take a polemic approach and its permanent collection does an excellent job of demonstrating that the development of indigenous art since the start of the 20th century has recorded, commented on and affected political events. All in all better than merely interesting it is an exciting place to visit.

name: Colonne Vendôme
description: The centrepiece of a magnificent 8-sided square first laid out in 1699 to show off an equestrian statue of the Sun King, Louis XIV. The statue was removed amid revolutionary fervor in 1792 and replaced in 1806 with the Colonne de la Grande Armée. This was modelled on Trajan's column in Rome and decorated with Napoleon's military exploits. The present column is a replica, however, as the original was pulled down during the 1871 Paris Commune. Place Vendôme represents the best of well-heeled Paris, being home to an abundance of exclusive boutiques, jewellers and fashion labels—Cartier, Boucheron, Trussardi, van Cleef & Arpels—several banks, the French Ministry of Justice, and the Hôtel Ritz.

The main axis of the neighbourhood, boulevard des États-Unis, was named to honour the United States, which had just entered World War I when the street was opened in 1917. 25 wall paintings made in the 1980s and 1990s show examples of Garnier's work and his "ideal city projects"; see also "Musée urbain Tony Garnier" in the museums section.

name: Ile Barbe
description: This charming island on the river Saône is the only inhabited island in Lyon. In the 5th century, one of the first monasteries in Gaul was founded there. It became a powerful Benedictine abbey (from the 9th century) but was finally ruined in 1526 by Protestants, during the religious wars. Of the three churches that existed on the island, only the Romanesque Notre-Dame remains. The island also has other old buildings in a quiet and green environment. The suspension bridge was built in 1827.

A strong testimony of this era remains in the form of massive Soviet-style buildings erected in the 1930s. The Gratte-Ciel ("skyscrapers") ensemble comprises the city hall, the National Popular Theatre and housing buildings, including the skyscrapers themselves. These are 19 stories high. name: Ponte Sant'Angelo
description: This is a footbridge connecting Castel Sant'Angelo with the other side of the Tiber. It is a Roman bridge completed in 134 AD by Hadrian, to give access to his newly constructed mausoleum. Pilgrims used this bridge to reach St Peter's Basilica, hence it was earlier known as the "bridge of Saint Peter". In the seventh century, the castle and the bridge took on the name Sant'Angelo, when it is said that an angel appeared on the roof of the castle to announce the end of a plague. The statues of ten angels on the bridge reflect its name.

name: Saint Mark's Basilica
description: Saint Mark's Basilica is on the Piazza San Marco and is one of the highlights of a visit to Venice. As with most churches in Italy, you must be dressed appropriately to be allowed in; this means no short skirts or bare shoulders. You are not allowed to carry large bags or rucksacks inside, sometimes even small daypacks may need to be deposited. Storage is available just around the corner from the main entrance (free of charge). Filming and photography is forbidden so be prepared in advance. The visit within the basilica lasts ten minutes. Waiting for entry into the basilica can last up to five or so hours and it may be wise to use a ticket service to reserve your visit (reservation costs €3…

name: S. Maria della Salute
description: As a votive offering for the city's deliverance from the Black Plague, the church was designed in the then fashionable Baroque style. Construction began in 1631. Most of the objects of art housed in the church bear references to the Black Death. description: The oldest and most celebrated bridge over the Arno, and the only Florentine bridge to survive World War II. The design is distinctive: it's a three-arched bridge supporting a parade of shops supporting another bridge. It's lined by shops, which were butchers until Renaissance times then - in an insight as dramatic as the discovery of perspective in painting - they realised that goldsmiths' shops paid higher rents and didn't stink; so from then to this day it's just been overpriced jewellery shops and market…

It was completely reconstructed by King Rama III in the early nineteenth century, and he renamed the temple Wat Yan Nawa (Boat Temple). The main feature of this temple is the base of the temple, that is shaped like a Chinese junk with two pagodas functioning as its masts. King Rama III saw that steam ships were slowly replacing old junks, and wanted the people to remember how much wealth they had brought to Siam. In the early nineteenth century, Chinese people started moving to the area, and the temple is still popular among the Chinese community residing there.

It is home to a variety of counterfeit merchandise including watches, clothing, bags, and cosmetics as well as Thai tourist products such as model tuk-tuks and kick-boxing shorts. The prices at this market are exorbitant and anyone brave enough to buy anything here should bargain extensively. Most items available at the Patpong Night Market are available for less than half the price at other locations in Bangkok.

name: Wat Chedi Luang
description: Almost in the centre of Chiang Mai are the remains of a massive chedi that toppled in the great earthquake of 1545. The temple was originally constructed in 1401 on the orders of King Saeng Muang Ma. In 1454, reigning King Tilo-Garaj enlarged the chedi (pronounced jedee) to a height of 86 m. After the earthquake, the chedi lay in ruins until 1991-92, when it was reconstructed at a cost of several million baht. A magnificent testament to Lanna (northern Thai) architecture and art, restored sections hint at its former glory. Wat Chedi Luang is also home to the "Pillar of the City", a totem used in ancient Thai fertility rites.

name: Wat Chiang Man
description: The oldest temple in the city. Presumed to date from the year Chiang Mai was founded (1296), it is famed for two Buddha statues, which are about 1,800 and 1,000 years old, respectively. King Mengrai allegedly lived here while the city of Chiang Mai was being constructed. Enshrined in Wat Chiang Man is a tiny crystal Buddha called Pra Seh-Taang Kamaneeee, which is thought to have the power to bring rain. Another image, called Phra Sila Khoa, reflects the fine workmanship of Indian craftsmen from thousands of years ago.

description: Completely rebuilt in 1884 after the disastrous earthquake of 1863, the seat of Manila's colonial-era city council once had some of the grandest interiors in Intramuros. The 1945 Battle of Manila left it a gutted shell, of which only parts of the first storey survived; it then suffered the indignity of serving as a parking lot. A major reconstruction project that started a few years ago is finally nearing completion, with the façade of the historic building now having regained much of its pre-war glory.

name: San Agustín Church
description: A true Spanish Baroque treasure, with magnificent trompe-l'œil ceilings and a splendid high altar. Consecrated in 1607, this ancient building managed to survive the Second World War (although it, too, sustained heavy damage) and is said to be the oldest stone church still standing in the Philippines. It was added to the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1993 as part of the group "Baroque Churches of the Philippines". Miguel López de Legazpi (1502-1572), the first Spanish Governor-General of the Philippines, is buried in a tomb near the high altar; other funerary monuments can be found along the walls or set into the floor. Much of San Agustín's neighbouring monastery was damaged during the war…

The museum exhibits the plight of jailed political revolutionaries under the French colonial regime and the struggle of the Vietnamese people against imperialism in chilling detail. name: Dai Nam Tourist Park
description: This is one of the largest tourist attractions in Vietnam. It features the Dai Nam Van Hien Temple, an entertainment site, open range zoo, shopping areas, hotels, local and Western cuisine, and the largest man-made mountain range in Vietnam. Costing over 50 billion dong to build, this park is the beginning of mass tourism in Vietnam, although it is aimed at tourists and locals, and comes highly recommended. Transport options to the park are quite convoluted. As the park is new, online information is scarce. According to the locals, it is very much worth a visit, purely just to view the temple.

name: Fort Cornwallis
description: The fort, named for Charles Cornwallis, is built on the site where Francis Light, founder of Penang, landed on 11 August 1786. It was first built in 1793. But this site was an unlikely spot to defend the city from invasion. In 1810 it was rebuilt in an attempt to make up for initial strategic planning errors. In the shape of a star, the only actual buildings still standing are the outer walls, a gunpowder magazine, and a small Christian chapel. Several old cannons (including one that is believed by some locals to have magical 'fertility' powers) can still be found at the fort. In 1836, construction of a new temple began and was completed eight years later. Fire razed the wooden structure to the ground in 1894, it was allegedly struck by lightning. Chinese believed that it was due to its resemblance to the Emperor's palace, which provoked the gods. A scaled-down version was later built in 1902 and completed in 1906. name: Dr Johnson's House
description: Dr Samuel Johnson was the highly distinguished 18th-century "man of letters", best known for his comprehensive English Dictionary of 1755, but also for his prolific output of poems, essays and novels. Something of a "hidden gem", this small, independent museum is dedicated to him—and, with its historic interiors, paintings and prints, personal effects and other exhibits—gives an impression of what it might have been like during his occupancy from 1748 to 1759. Built in 1700, this impressive period building—a rare example of its kind in the area—survived the brutal onslaught of the Blitz during World War II and is now maintained in excellent condition.

name: London Mithraeum
description: The London Mithraeum is a 3rd-century Roman mithraeum that was discovered in Walbrook during construction work in 1954. The entire site was relocated several times before being returned to its original site as part of the new Bloomberg building. This temple of the mystery god Mithras became perhaps the most famous 20th-century Roman discovery in London. In addition to the temple structure, there is a display of Roman artefacts found on the site and a contemporary art exhibit responding to the site. Visitor numbers are limited and timed slots are often fully booked up several weeks in advance, so plan well ahead.

name: James Clerk Maxwell's Birthplace
description: Isaac Newton realised that what caused the apple to fall was the very same force moving the moon, planets and stars. James Clerk Maxwell (1831-1879) was born in this house, before the family moved to Kirkcudbright. He was intensely curious about how nature worked and made a "great unification" of equal importance to Newton's: that magnetism, electricity, light and heat are all manifestations of the same electromagnetic spectrum. And this spectrum must contain other frequencies beyond human sensing: hence X-rays and radio waves, and the entire science of telecommunications. He made possible Einstein's 20th century unification of gravity, mass and energy, and contributed to many other fields…

name: Dean Village
description: It is an attractive hamlet down in the dene - the steep valley - of the Water of Leith. It was the medieval crossing point on the route from Edinburgh to South Queensferry, and is the main access point for this section of the Water of Leith Walkway (described below). The fast-descending stream drove 11 grain mills here, so it was the powerbase for the Baxters, the bakers' merchant guild. The present bridge across the stream was built in the 18th century, only just wide enough for a horse and cart. name: Lisbon Botanical Gardens
description: A hidden gem. It was created several hundred years ago, by a King of Portugal at the time of the Discoveries. The story goes that this King wanted one of every type of plant in the world, and although that's unlikely, there is a huge collection dating back by three or four centuries which is worth checking out. And there's something quite eerie about seeing plants or huge trees from completely different climates growing next to each other in apparent harmony. A great place to take a picnic: this green oasis is completely surrounded by city but even the city sounds filter out.

name: Miradouro da Senhora do Monte
description: The highest viewpoint in Lisbon, at the top of the Graça hill, spread out in front of the small Capela de Nossa Senhora do Monte (founded in 1147, remodelled in the 20th century). To the south you look down over the Castelo de São Jorge, the Mouraria and the Baixa to the Tagus estuary; to the west, from Bairro Alto out to the Monsanto forest; to the north, down the Avenida Almirante Reis valley. It sits a little further out than the viewpoints at Santa Luzia and Portas do Sol, so it is usually quieter, and it is a fine place to watch the sunset.

The church was preserved that way and now serves as the Museu Arqueológico in the extant parts of the building. The museum houses a hodgepodge of archaeological artifacts from around Portugal and the world including mummies from South America, tombs of Portuguese rulers, and the Stations of the Cross on 18th-century painted tiles. description: This is a historic aqueduct in the city of Lisbon, Portugal. It is one of the most remarkable examples of 18th-century Portuguese engineering, including the largest stone arch in the world. The main course of the aqueduct covers 18 km, but the whole network of canals extends through nearly 58 km. The Mãe d'Água (Mother of the Water) reservoir of the Amoreiras, the largest of the water reservoirs, was finished in 1834. This reservoir, with a capacity of 5,500 m³ of water, was designed by Carlos Mardel. It is now deactivated and can be visited as part of the Museu da Água (Water Museum).

name: Frauenkirche
description: This huge church defines the Munich skyline with its twin onion-domed towers, a shade over 98 m tall - the money ran out for the planned spires. It's the Roman Catholic cathedral, but always known locally as Frauenkirche. It was built from 1469 to 1488 in brick because of a lack of suitable local stone; the towers were only completed in 1525, cleverly anticipating a law of 2004 that no structure within Altstadt may exceed 99 m in height. Although its style is Gothic, it's fairly simple outside and in, without the usual ornamentation of that style. Eleven kings or archdukes of Bavaria are interred here. name: Michaelskirche
description: Grand Renaissance church built for the Jesuits 1583-1599 by Duke Wilhelm V, as a bastion of the Counter-Reformation against those awful Lutherans. The Duke nearly busted the state coffers in buying up the land and funding a construction that townsfolk reckoned was too big to stand. And down fell the tower: "I know, I'll build it bigger". This version survived until bombed in wartime and was restored in the 1950s. The facade and interior continue the triumphal theme, for example the statue of Archangel Michael slaying a demon who might be Protestant. The church crypt holds many tombs of the Wittelsbach dynasty, including "mad king" Ludwig II.

description: This Late Baroque confection was built from 1733 to 1746 as a private chapel by Egid Quirin Asam - he could see the altar from his house next door. His brother, Cosmas Damian Asam, did the frescoes. The church is dedicated to St John Nepomuk (1345-93), a Bohemian monk cast into the river Vltava in Prague at the behest of King Wenceslaus IV. Legend has it that Nepomuk refused to divulge the queen's confessional secrets, but his real crime was to back the wrong candidate for abbot. The church is wonderful by candlelight, especially at the Christmas Eve service, replete with Bavarian singers in the choir stall.

description: This neo-Romanesque church was completed in 1895, one of a trio commissioned for the expanding district of Maxvorstadt. It was bombed in wartime but rebuilt to the original design. He kept siding with the wrong king and the wrong pope, and when ousted hurled the cathedral keys into the Elbe. But later they turned up in his fish supper, whereupon regal order, apostolic succession and church access were serenely restored.

description: This was established in 1563 when plague overfilled the church graveyards, and bodies needed to be interred beyond city limits. From 1788 to 1868 it was Munich's single collective burial ground, becoming non-denominational, so it's the last resting-place of some 14,000 citizens. The roll-call includes Josef von Fraunhofer, Friedrich von Gärtner, Leo von Klenze, Justus von Liebig, Georg Simon Ohm and Carl Spitzweg. The Acropolis is considered to be an enduring symbol of Western civilisation.

name: Pnyx
description: If Athens is the birthplace of democracy, then Pnyx is its cradle. Around 507 BCE this rocky hill, overlooking the Akropolis, became the meeting place for the ekklesia, Athens' early democratic assembly. This site thus witnessed addresses by Pericles, Aristides and Alcibiades during the "Golden Age" of Athens, and had a capacity for 6000 to 13,000 hearers. The site was redesigned several times, creating three distinct phases in its history, until the ekklesia moved to the Theatre of Dionysos some time during the first century BCE. During the Roman era Pnyx was instead used as a sanctuary of Zeus.

name: Stephansdom
description: Yet another patchwork of architectural styles, but predominantly Gothic. None of the original construction remains, the oldest extant sections are the thirteenth century Giant Gate (Riesentor) and Towers of the Heathens (Heidentürme), both of which are Romanesque. In 1511, building in Gothic style ceased due to being out of fashion. The main altar has a Baroque panel showing St. Stephen, Christianity's first martyr. The organised tour is worth it, since some of the finest works of art in the cathedral can only be seen with a guide, such as Emperor Frederick III's red marble sepulcher and the immense Gothic carved Altar of Wiener Neustadt. Those interested in attending Mass may come Saturday…

name: Wiener Staatsoper
description: Probably the most-beloved symbol of Viennese arts, and one of the first buildings to be rebuilt in the postwar era. It was built from 1861-1869 under the direction of architects Eduard van der Nüll and August von Siccardsburg for then-emperor Franz Josef I. The first performance was Don Giovanni, an opera by Austrian native Mozart, on 25 May 1869. The architecture of the opera was barely tolerated by the picky Viennese when it opened. Van der Nüll did not take these criticisms of his work lightly and committed suicide. A few weeks later, von Siccardsburg died of a heart attack. Doubly cursed, the opera building succumbed to bombs less than 100 years later, during World War II. After ten yea…

Materials such as bronze, limestone, marble, tiles, and translucent glass create a sense of enduring quality. This set off a few furious years of archaeological digging, resulting in a rather surprising (and extremely significant) discovery that nested underneath the original Aztec temple was six distinct smaller, older temples. You can see each layer walking through the dig site.

name: Café El Jarocho
description: This is a very old, family-owned coffee roaster's shop, and there are now at least three locations in Coyoacán. They have really good and cheap coffee, bad and cheap tortas (sandwiches in French bread), and reasonably standard American-style donuts. There are benches on the sidewalk just outside the Jarocho shops where you can sit to drink your coffee, or you can do like everyone else in Coyoacán and just stroll around the park with your Jarocho foam cup in your hand. On weekends, expect to wait in line to order your coffee. A long wait in line for coffee, a bag of fresh churros, and a conversation in Coyoacán's plaza is a quintessential Mexico City date.

name: Museo Vivo del Muralismo
description: This museum is housed in a former convent from 1729 that later became headquarters for the Education Secretariat. In 1923, the department commissioned the up-and-coming Diego Rivera to decorate the building with 124 mural panels, extending over two city blocks and filling three levels. There are elaborate panels of traditional Mexican life on the ground floor, state seals on the second floor, and themes of revolution and class inequality on the third level. There is also a David Alfaro Siqueiros mural in the main stairwell. In 2024, the building became a museum dedicated to Mexican murals, with additional exhibits. Photography permitted, no flash.

name: Museo Memoria y Tolerancia
description: Opened in 2010, this museum is dedicated to the remembrance of genocides and crimes against humanity committed around the globe, with the goal of promoting peace and tolerance. Separate sections of the museum are devoted to the Holocaust, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Rwanda, the Khmer Rouge, Darfur, Armenia, and Guatemala. Genocide is only one of the issues the museum confronts. Exhibits also explore hate crimes committed in the name of religion, racial purity, and especially sexual orientation, with a number of exhibits and lectures exploring LGBT issues (in Mexico, they tend to add a lot of extra letters so that you might see it as LGBTTTQIA).

description: A few km north of the beach, this mountainous subtropical forest is Brazil's smallest national park. It is largely hand-planted as much of the original forest was destroyed to make way for coffee plantations. Despite this it contains hundreds of species, many of which are threatened with extinction. Corcovado is to the east of the park but if you really want to appreciate what the park has to offer you have to drive along some windy, hilly roads and get out and hike. This sector of the park can be reached via Rua Boa Vista, and from São Conrado in Zona Oeste.

name: Bradleys Head

There's pristine bushland (almost unchanged from the time of European colonisation), quiet beaches, and knockout views across the harbour, and in the warmer months you'll spot plenty of Eastern Water Dragons, a type of large lizard. Once you reach the tip of the headland, you can either amble back to the wharf or - if you're feeling more ambitious - follow the track several more kilometres to Clifton Gardens, ogling the gigantic houses along the way. From there, you can either hike all the way back to Taronga or get a bus to a ferry wharf.

The remains of the building were excavated after rediscovery in 1983 and the original foundations can now be viewed through glass floor panels in the museum. Fascinating changing exhibitions of art and photography, films and state-of-the-art technology spin stories of colonial life, Aboriginal culture, environment, trade, authority / law and everyday dramas and dreams in early Sydney. The Museum of Sydney Cafe, by the museum entrance is not really part of the museum, and is much more a restaurant than a cheap and casual cafe.

name: Cadman's Cottage
description: The last relic of the small, relatively plain buildings that once ringed Sydney Cove in the early colonial period, this small sandstone cottage was built in 1815-1816. The building has survived largely because of constant government or institutional ownership. Restoration began in 1972 and the building is now used as an information centre by the National Parks and Wildlife Service. The Cottage was built by the water side, but with reclamation over the years, the shoreline of Sydney Cove is now 100 metres distant.

description: Follow Argyle St through this historic sandstone road cutting made between 1843 and 1867, made with the effort of both convict and paid labour. name: Sydney Observatory
description: Australia's oldest observatory. It has a variety of exhibitions, a “beanbag planetarium” and of course, telescopes. The parks and views of the harbour from the Observatory Hill are exceptional. It's worth a visit even if you have no interest in astronomy and are not even going into the building. You can book a night tour guided by an astronomer, where you're allowed to use the telescope and see what is visible during night time. The old telescopes here aren't the most powerful around; the portable telescopes set up are just as powerful as the large ones in the domes. It makes for a fun, informative night out. Children are catered for in both the daytime and evening sessions.

name: Akshardham
description: Completed in 2005 by the socio-spiritual organisation BAPS, no expense has been spared in decorating this large and elaborate temple carved of red sandstone. The central monument, built without any steel, houses an 11-ft golden statue of the founder of the Swaminarayan faith, Bhagwan Swaminarayan. The Premvati food court on the grounds serves up fast, cheap, huge but mediocre portions of vegetarian food, ₹75 for a thali. There is a strict ban on all electronic items, cameras, tobacco and pretty much everything except the clothes on your back. You can leave your belongings in the cloakroom outside. Allow at least three-four hours to explore it all.

name: Red Fort
description: One of Delhi's top tourist sights and listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. A brilliant red sandstone fort was built by the Mughal Emperor Shah Jahan (who also built the Taj Mahal) as his ruling palace. Completed in 1648, the years since have not treated the buildings kindly: the rooms have long since been stripped of all objects, the marble inlays are long gone and quite a few buildings are off-limits. Still, the scale remains imposing and the gardens are kept lush and green even in midwinter.

description: Feroz Shah Kotla is the fifth citadel of Delhi and was built by Feroz Shah Tughlaq in 1354. The previous citadels of Delhi were abandoned due to lack of water, so Feroz Shah Kotla was built right next to the Yamuna River. Today the ruins of Feroz Shah Kotla lie nestled between the cricket stadium, of the same name, and the Ring Road. The ruins of the Feroze Shah Kotla are said to be the abode of friendly djinns (spirit) and every Thursday hordes of devotees, irrespective of religion, visit the ruins of Feroz Shah Kotla with photocopies of letters, citing their problems. name: Hawa Mahal
description: Hawa Mahal or Kushk-i-Shikar lies on the northern end of the citadel and is crowned with the Ashokan Pillar (Minar-e-Zarreen). It is built with a central solid core and vaulted cells around it. Stairs at the corners lead to the uppermost terrace where the Ashokan pillar is planted. The pillar was originally from Topar in Ambala. It was shifted to the present location by Feroz Shah Tughlaq. The pillar has inscription in the Prakrit language. Stairs lead to the very top of the stepped pyramid providing close views of the inscription of the pillar along with a bird's eye view of the entire complex and beyond.

description: It is an Anglican church, built in 1836 by Colonel James Skinner. It is one of the oldest churches in the city. It was designed by Major Robert Smith. Construction started in 1826 and completed in 1936. The design follows the Renaissance Revival architectural style and the church is laid out on a cruciform plan. The church has three porticoed porches and is crowned with a central octagonal dome. The dome is topped with a copper ball topped with a cross. The interior of St James' Church are laid out with beautiful stained glass windows depicting the crucifixion, ascension of Christ and his resurrection. name: Albert Hall Museum
description: A fine example of Indo-Saracenic architecture, this building was designed by Sir Samuel Swinton Jacob and was opened as public museum in 1887. Maharaja Ram Singh wanted this building to be a town hall, but his successor, Madho Singh II, decided it should be a museum for the art of Jaipur and included as part of the new Ram Nivas Garden. The museum has a rich collection of artefacts like paintings, carpets, ivory, stone, metal sculptures and colourful crystal works. It is named after King Edward VII (Albert Edward), during whose visit to the city as the Prince of Wales, its foundation stone was laid on 6 February 1876.

name: Hagia Sophia
description: The third and grandest of the churches on this site, completed in 537 AD. The 30-m diameter dome covers what was for over 1000 years the largest enclosed space in the world, only surpassed in 1520 by Seville cathedral. It used "pendentive" architecture to throw the dome's weight onto four stout pillars, a design that inspired many Eastern Orthodox churches and Ottoman mosques. It became a mosque after the Ottoman conquest in 1453, remaining so until 1931. It was then a museum until 2020 when it was again proclaimed a mosque. That means you must work around prayer times and dress appropriately. Very cheap disposable headscarves are available for purchase outside the building.

name: Palace of the Porphyrogenitus
description: The Byzantines built several great palaces in Constantinople and this is the only one to survive almost intact. It's from the late 13th century, in typical alternating marble and red-brick rows, and was an imperial residence: Porphyrogenitus means "born to the purple" indicating the heir to the crown. Yet it was merely an annex or pavilion within the much greater Palace of Blachernae, of which nothing else remains. It's set within the north end of the Theodosian Walls and was much bashed during the Ottoman capture. Later it was variously a menagerie, brothel, pottery, poorhouse and bottle works, then fell derelict in the 20th century. In 2021 it re-opened as a museum.

description: The building was erected as a Roman Catholic church in 1325 by the friars of the Dominican Order, near or above an earlier chapel dedicated to Saint Paul (Italian: San Paolo) in 1233. In 1299, the Dominican Friar Guillaume Bernard de Sévérac bought a house near the church, where he established a monastery with 12 friars. A new, much larger church was built near or above the chapel of San Paolo in 1325. Thereafter the church was officially dedicated to San Domenico. description: Markets of Marrakech, just adjacent to Place Djemaa El-Fna, are where you can buy almost anything, from spices to shoes, jellabas to kaftans, and tea pots to tagines. Undoubtedly, being a foreigner means you will end up paying higher prices than a native would, but be sure to bargain nonetheless. If you happen to run out of dirham, you will also find plenty of people in the souks who will eagerly exchange your dollars or euros (though a fair rate here is less likely than at an official exchange). All that said, the sellers here are much less aggressive than, say, Egypt, so have fun!

name: Koutoubia Mosque
description: Named after the booksellers market that used to be located here. It is said that the minaret of the Koutoubia mosque is to Marrakech as the Eiffel Tower is to Paris. The minaret is visible from Gueliz which is connected to the Medina by Avenue Mohammed V. At night, the mosque is beautifully lit. The Almohad caliph Abd al-Mu'min founded the first mosque here in 1147 and built the present one beside it in 1158; the excavated remains of the first mosque can be seen on the esplanade next to it. The minaret was completed under Caliph Yaqub al-Mansur (1184 to 1199), and has inspired other buildings such as the Giralda of Seville and the Hassan Tower of Rabat. Non-Muslims are not allowed inside.

name: Saadian Tombs
description: Saadian Tombs. The tombs were built in the 16th century as the dynastic necropolis of the Saadian dynasty. The complex includes the Chamber of the Twelve Columns, the Chamber of the Mihrab, the Chamber of the Three Niches and the garden tombs. The site was rediscovered in 1917 and subsequently restored and opened to visitors. The site is relatively compact and most visitors can see the main areas in 20–30 minutes. The Chamber of the Twelve Columns cannot be entered: visitors look in from an opening at its edge, originally a window in the eastern wall, and often have to wait for a turn. The entrance passage is narrow, so arriving early can help avoid queues.

name: El Bahia Palace
description: An ornate palace complex built in the late 19th century, with courtyards, gardens, richly decorated rooms and traditional Moroccan architectural details. The palace was begun in the 1860s by Si Moussa, grand vizier to Sultan Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman, and greatly expanded in 1894–1900 by his son Ba Ahmed, Grand Vizier to Sultan Moulay Abdelaziz. The main complex covers almost 2 hectares and has about 150 rooms. The main entrance is on Rue Riad Zitoun el Jedid. The palace is relatively close to other attractions in the southern Medina and can be reached on foot from Jemaa el-Fnaa. Arriving shortly after opening can be useful for visitors who want to avoid the busiest periods.

name: The Chapel Bridge
description: The Chapel Bridge was built in the 14th century to aid in the protection of the city. It is a landmark of Lucerne and is said to be the oldest wooden bridge in all of Europe. A point of interest as you walk over it are the paintings in the rafters depicting 12th-century city life and Swiss history. The bridge was badly damaged by a fire on 18 August 1993; it was rebuilt within a year, but the damage is still visible in places and many of the original paintings were lost. The tower which has had multiple uses over the years (including as a dungeon) is still in the original condition, but not open for visitors.

name: The Lion Monument
description: Also known as the Lion of Lucerne, it is a sculpture designed by Bertel Thorvaldsen. It commemorates the Swiss Guards who were massacred in 1792 during the French Revolution, when revolutionaries stormed the Tuileries Palace in Paris, France. The American writer Mark Twain (1835–1910) praised the sculpture of a mortally-wounded lion as "the most mournful and moving piece of stone in the world.". The sculpture is a popular sight with a constant flow of tour groups arriving during the day - visit early or late in the day if possible for a more peaceful experience.

name: Mount Pilatus
description: A famous mountain overlooking the city of Lucerne. Pilatus is definitely a must and gives you a good impression of a wild and rocky peak with a marvelous view of the "real" Alps. Its peak can be reached by the world's steepest cogwheel railway from Alpnachstad (not operating in wintertime) and all-year-round by cable-car in three sections from Kriens (10 minutes by trolley bus no. 1 from Lucerne as far as 'Linde/Pilatus'). Going up from Alpnachstad and down to Kriens, combined with a boat ride from Lucerne, is called the Golden Round Trip and is over €100. A pleasant, and cheaper, option is to take the train from Lucerne to Alpnachstad (roughly €8), then take the cogwheel railway to Pilatus…

It's an iconic bridge that consists of nine arches and a drawbridge that is still operated by hand. The current bridge is made of white-painted wood, but it has been rebuilt several times and historically it has also been in concrete. The first bridge here was built in 1691, but the current one dates from 1934. It is one of the most photographed bridges in Amsterdam, especially at night because of the 1200 tiny lights that make it look like a picture-perfect postcard.

The building has been closed to the public since 9/11.

description: Tex-mex, casual dining
transit: Open public transport directions from your starting point to compare available routes and current service.

name: McMurdo Station
description: The largest community and logistical hub on Antarctica, situated on the bare volcanic rock of Hut Point Peninsula on Ross Island with laboratories, dormitories, and panoramic views of Mount Discovery.
transit: Access strictly via expedition vessel, ski-equipped aircraft, or authorized research logistics.
driving: Specialized tracked polar vehicles operate locally; visitor transport is coordinated by station operations.

name: Discovery Hut
description: Historic wooden hut erected in 1902 by Captain Robert Falcon Scott during the British National Antarctic Discovery Expedition, preserved as an Antarctic historic monument with original expedition supplies.
transit: Short walking path along Hut Point from central McMurdo Station.
driving: Walk from McMurdo Station or Scott Base; vehicles are restricted around the historic perimeter.

name: Observation Hill
description: A steep 230-meter volcanic cone rising adjacent to McMurdo Station, topped with a commemorative wooden cross for Scott’s party and offering 360-degree vistas across the Ross Ice Shelf and Erebus ice tongue.
transit: Marked trail ascending directly from McMurdo Station.
driving: Foot ascent only via the marked switchback trail; dress for sudden wind chill.

name: Port Lockroy & Bransfield House
description: The historic British Base A established during Operation Tabarin in 1944 on Goudier Island, home to the world’s southernmost functioning public post office, museum, and a gentoo penguin colony.
transit: Zodiac tender landing from expedition cruise vessels visiting the Wiencke Island harbor.
driving: No vehicle roads; exploration is conducted on designated foot pathways across Goudier Island.

name: Jougla Point
description: A rocky peninsula forming the western side of the entrance to Alice Creek in Port Lockroy, celebrated for massive whale bone skeletons, resting Weddell seals, and nesting colonies of blue-eyed shags.
transit: Zodiac tender landing from vessels anchored in Port Lockroy.
driving: Foot travel along rocky shoreline; maintain respectful distance from wildlife.

name: Whalers Bay Historic Station
description: Atmospheric bay inside Deception Island’s volcanic caldera, featuring black volcanic sand beaches, steam rising from thermal waters, and the rusted iron ruins of the early 20th-century Hektor Whaling Station.
transit: Expedition ship entry through Neptune’s Bellows followed by zodiac beach landing.
driving: Walking on volcanic ash beach; watch for hot volcanic ground and geothermal steam.

name: Baily Head Chinstrap Colony
description: A dramatic natural amphitheater of black volcanic cinder on the eastern headland of Deception Island, hosting one of the largest breeding populations of chinstrap penguins in the world with over 100,000 pairs.
transit: Expedition zodiac landing on the outer surf beach when sea conditions permit.
driving: Strictly on foot; landing requires moderate surf navigation and guided wildlife approach.

name: Amundsen-Scott South Pole Station
description: The premier scientific laboratory situated at the exact Geographic South Pole at an elevation of 2,835 meters, supporting astrophysics research including the IceCube Neutrino Observatory.
transit: Ski-equipped LC-130 Hercules or Twin Otter flight from Union Glacier camp.
driving: Snowmobiles and specialized low-pressure tire vehicles operate on groomed polar skiways.

name: Nyroysa Coastal Terrace
description: The sole practical ice-free coastal terrace on the world’s most isolated island, created by volcanic rockfall in the 1950s and serving as a haven for Antarctic fur seals, elephant seals, and macaroni penguins.
transit: Helicopter transfer from specialized polar expedition vessel.
driving: No vehicle infrastructure; access is strictly pedestrian with Norwegian Polar Institute authorization.

name: Cape Circoncision
description: The historic northwestern headland of Bouvet Island first sighted on New Year’s Day 1739 by French navigator Jean-Baptiste Bouvet de Lozier, surrounded by towering glacial sea cliffs and dramatic swells.
transit: Offshore expedition vessel viewing or zodiac shoreline patrol.
driving: Inaccessible to ground vehicles; steep glacier-capped basalt cliffs drop straight to sea level.

name: Diego Garcia Lagoon
description: An immense, protected coral atoll lagoon spanning over 120 square kilometers of turquoise waters, home to intact coral reefs, spinner dolphins, sea turtles, and vibrant pelagic fish species.
transit: Internal service boat or authorized military transport across the lagoon.
driving: Paved ring road links major sectors along the narrow western atoll rim.

name: East Point Historic Plantation
description: Historic settlement on the eastern arm of Diego Garcia featuring preserved colonial stone administrative buildings, coconut processing mills, and historic cemeteries dating to the 19th and 20th centuries.
transit: Service vehicles or bicycles along the eastern atoll road.
driving: Follow East Point Road south from the main station area; road conditions vary.

name: Salomon Atoll & Boddam Island
description: An untouched circular atoll ring in the northern Chagos Archipelago, known among global yacht navigators for crystal clear lagoon anchorages, lush coconut palms, and pristine fringing barrier reefs.
transit: Private ocean-going yacht anchoring in the protected northern lagoon passage.
driving: No vehicle roads; dinghy ashore and explore footpaths through the coconut groves.

name: Atlas Cove ANARE Station Site
description: The historic base of the Australian National Antarctic Research Expeditions (ANARE) occupied from 1947 to 1954, nestled between Corinthian Bay and Atlas Roadstead beneath glacier-clad volcanic cliffs.
transit: Small boat or amphibious vehicle landing from research expedition vessel.
driving: No roads; traverse the gravel moraine and moss banks on foot.

name: Big Ben Volcano & Mawson Peak
description: Rising to 2,745 meters, Big Ben is an active sub-Antarctic ice-covered stratovolcano and the highest mountain on Australian territory, dominating the island with glistening glaciers and volcanic steam plumes.
transit: Viewed from expedition vessels offshore or from landing points at Spit Bay and Atlas Cove.
driving: Severe glacial terrain; access requires specialized mountaineering permits and polar equipment.

name: Nukunonu Lagoon & Coral Gardens
description: Tokelau’s largest coral lagoon bordered by more than twenty idyllic islets (motu), featuring turquoise waters, vibrant coral bommies, giant clams, and serene outrigger canoeing routes.
transit: Traditional wooden outrigger canoes or small aluminum dinghies connecting village islets.
driving: No car traffic; walkable sandy trails along the residential motu.

name: Atafu Traditional Polynesian Village
description: A close-knit Polynesian community on the northernmost atoll of Tokelau, famous for historic coral-stone church architecture, sustainable kanava wood canoe carving, and traditional communal fishing.
transit: Passenger ship from Apia, Samoa, arriving fortnightly; local reef boat crossing to shore.
driving: Pleasant shaded village walking paths surfaced with crushed coral sand.

name: Fakaofo Fale Fono
description: The historic village meeting house on Fale islet, serving as the cultural and political center of Fakaofo where local council meetings (Taupulega), song celebrations, and choral events take place.
transit: Inter-island passenger ferry from Samoa with local reef transfer.
driving: All travel within the compact village islet is on foot.

name: Battle of Midway National Memorial
description: A national memorial honoring the pivotal naval battle of June 1942 that shaped the Pacific theater, featuring historic seaplane hangars, anti-aircraft gun emplacements, and commemorative monuments.
transit: Charter flight to Henderson Field on Sand Island or authorized vessel anchorage.
driving: Bicycles and small electric utility golf carts provide transport around Sand Island.

name: Sand Island Albatross Sanctuary
description: The world’s largest breeding colony of Laysan albatrosses and black-footed albatrosses, where hundreds of thousands of birds nest among native naupaka shrubs along white sand coral beaches.
transit: Walk or bicycle from central accommodations on Sand Island.
driving: Low speed electric vehicles permitted on designated perimeter roads.

name: Palmyra Atoll Marine Sanctuary
description: One of the most pristine and untouched coral atoll marine ecosystems on Earth, co-managed by The Nature Conservancy and USFWS with lush Pisonia grandis rainforests, blacktip reef sharks, and seabird colonies.
transit: Charter research flight landing on Cooper Island airstrip or authorized yacht mooring.
driving: Walking trails and small electric utility vehicles along Cooper Island causeways.

name: Wake Island WWII Memorial
description: Commemorating the gallant defense of Wake Island by US Marines and civilian contractors in December 1941, featuring preserved 5-inch naval gun batteries, bunker ruins, and historic air terminal artifacts.
transit: Air transport to Wake Island Airfield operated by the US Air Force.
driving: Station utility trucks and bicycles link Wake, Wilkes, and Peale islets.

name: Texas State Capitol
description: The monumental Italian Renaissance Revival statehouse completed in 1888 from sunset red granite, standing taller than the US Capitol in Washington DC amid 22 tree-shaded downtown park acres.
transit: CapMetro bus lines 1, 3, 7, 10, or 801 to Congress Avenue & 11th Street.
driving: Use the Capitol Visitors Parking Garage at 1201 San Jacinto Blvd; first two hours free.

name: Barton Springs Pool
description: A beloved three-acre natural limestone pool fed by underground freshwater springs that maintain a refreshing 68°F (20°C) year-round temperature, nestled in Zilker Metropolitan Park.
transit: CapMetro bus line 30 directly to Barton Springs / Zilker Park.
driving: Park at the dedicated Zilker Barton Springs lot off Barton Springs Road.

name: Lady Bird Lake Trail & Boardwalk
description: A scenic 10-mile trail and over-water boardwalk winding along the Colorado River in the heart of Austin, perfect for jogging, strolling, paddleboarding, and viewing the downtown skyline.
transit: CapMetro transit lines to South Congress or Riverside Drive, then walk to trailhead.
driving: Park at Lakeshore Drive or festival beach lots along the southern lake shore.

name: South Congress Avenue (SoCo)
description: Austin’s signature vibrant promenade packed with eclectic boutiques, vintage record shops, live music venues like the Continental Club, artisan eateries, and postcard views of the Capitol.
transit: CapMetro Rapid line 801 or bus lines 1 and 7 along South Congress.
driving: Metered street parking and paid neighborhood garages available behind Congress Ave.

name: Mount Bonnell
description: Considered Austin’s highest point at 775 feet above sea level, featuring a stone staircase leading to panoramic summit vistas over Lake Austin, surrounding hill country, and downtown.
transit: Rideshare or personal vehicle recommended; public transit is limited near the park entrance.
driving: Free public parking lot at Mount Bonnell Park entrance off Mount Bonnell Road.

name: Space Center Houston
description: The official visitor center of NASA Johnson Space Center, featuring Apollo 17, the giant Saturn V rocket, shuttle replica Independence mounted on the historic NASA 905 aircraft, and astronaut gear.
transit: Metro bus 249 or direct regional shuttles from downtown Houston.
driving: Follow I-45 South to NASA Parkway; large dedicated on-site parking available.

name: Houston Museum of Natural Science
description: A world-class institution in Hermann Park housing the Paleontology Hall with dynamic dinosaur fossils, the Burke Baker Planetarium, Cullen Hall of Gems & Minerals, and Cockrell Butterfly Center.
transit: METRORail Red Line to Museum District Station, followed by a 5-minute park walk.
driving: Dedicated multi-story parking garage at Caroline St and Hermann Drive.

name: Buffalo Bayou Park & Cistern
description: A 160-acre green corridor featuring winding bayou hiking trails, skyline overlooks, bat viewing at Waugh Drive Bridge, and the subterranean 1926 historic water reservoir known as The Cistern.
transit: METRO bus lines 40 or 41 along Memorial Drive and Allen Parkway.
driving: Park at The Water Works at Buffalo Bayou Park (105 Sabine St).

name: The Menil Collection
description: Renzo Piano-designed museum campus surrounded by tranquil neighborhood bungalows, housing John and Dominique de Menil’s premier collection of modern, surrealist, Byzantine, and African art.
transit: METRO bus 25 to Richmond & Yupon, then a brief northward stroll.
driving: Free visitor parking lot on West Alabama Street directly opposite the main building.

name: Dealey Plaza & The Sixth Floor Museum
description: A National Historic Landmark district in downtown Dallas and the former Texas School Book Depository, chronicling the life, presidency, and November 1963 assassination of John F. Kennedy.
transit: DART Light Rail (Red, Blue, Green, Orange) to West End Station.
driving: Multiple paid surface lots and garages around Elm and Houston Streets.

name: Dallas Arboretum and Botanical Garden
description: A 66-acre botanical garden perched on the southeastern shore of White Rock Lake, showcasing spectacular seasonal floral festivals, manicured tree canopies, and water sculptures.
transit: DART bus 214 connects to the arboretum gates on Garland Road.
driving: On-site paid parking garage with pedestrian tunnel directly into the gardens.

name: Klyde Warren Park
description: An innovative 5.2-acre deck park built over the recessed Woodall Rodgers Freeway, connecting the Dallas Arts District with uptown and hosting food trucks, live performances, and games.
transit: M-Line Vintage Trolley to Olive Street or DART rail to St. Paul Station.
driving: Park in nearby Arts District underground garages along Pearl or Olive Street.

name: The Alamo
description: The historic Spanish mission church founded in 1718 as Misión San Antonio de Valero and battlefield of the legendary 1836 siege, preserved at the center of Alamo Plaza with museum exhibits.
transit: VIA Metropolitan Transit routes 9, 14, 28 to Alamo Plaza.
driving: Park at the Houston Street Garage or Riverbend Garage two blocks away.

name: San Antonio River Walk (Paseo del Rio)
description: A tranquil pedestrian network of stone pathways, cypress trees, and arched footbridges situated one story below street level along the San Antonio River, lined with open-air cafes and barge tours.
price: Free to walk; river barge tours $14
transit: VIA Primo 100 or VIVA routes to downtown center, then take stairways down to the river.
driving: Central downtown parking garages on Commerce or Market Street.

name: San Antonio Missions National Historical Park
description: Texas’s only UNESCO World Heritage Site preserving four 18th-century Spanish frontier mission compounds along the river: Concepción, San José, San Juan Capistrano, and Espada.
transit: VIA route 42 to Mission San José visitor center.
driving: Drive Mission Road south from downtown; ample free parking at each mission site.

name: Griffith Observatory
description: Southern California’s iconic Art Deco observatory crowning Mount Hollywood, offering public telescopes, the Samuel Oschin Planetarium, and breathtaking views of the Hollywood Sign and LA basin.
transit: Metro B Line (Red) to Vermont/Sunset, then transfer to the DASH Observatory bus.
driving: Pay-by-the-hour parking lots along East Observatory Road, or free parking at the Greek Theatre when no events.

name: Santa Monica Pier & Pacific Park
description: The historic double-jointed wooden pier marking the western end of Route 66, complete with the solar-powered Pacific Wheel Ferris wheel, historic carousel, street musicians, and sweeping coastal vistas.
transit: Metro E Line (Expo) directly to Downtown Santa Monica Station, then walk 5 minutes west.
driving: City parking structures along 2nd and 4th Streets or the pier deck parking area.

name: The Getty Center
description: Richard Meier-designed travertine campus perched high above the Brentwood hills, housing European masterworks including Van Gogh’s Irises, expansive Central Garden, and vistas extending to the Pacific.
transit: Metro Bus 761 stops directly at the Getty Center tram arrival station on Sepulveda Blvd.
driving: Underground parking garage at 1200 Getty Center Drive, then ride the free computerized tram to summit.

name: Venice Beach Boardwalk & Canals
description: Eclectic bohemian coastal strip celebrated for Muscle Beach, street performers, skate park tricks, quirky vendor stalls, and the picturesque pedestrian Venice Canals built in 1905 by Abbot Kinney.
transit: Big Blue Bus route 1 or Metro Bus 33 to Venice & Windward.
driving: Paid beach parking lots at Rose Ave, Venice Blvd, or Washington Blvd.

name: Balboa Park
description: A 1,200-acre historic urban cultural park renowned for Spanish Colonial Revival palaces, the iconic Botanical Building and lily pond, 17 museums, lush canyon walking paths, and the Old Globe Theatre.
price: Park grounds & gardens free; museums ticketed
transit: MTS Bus routes 7 or 215 from downtown San Diego directly to Park Blvd.
driving: Multiple free public parking lots throughout the park grounds, including Inspiration Point.

name: USS Midway Museum
description: Historic naval aircraft carrier docked along Navy Pier in downtown San Diego, featuring over 30 restored aircraft on the four-acre flight deck, engine rooms, sleeping quarters, and pilot bridge.
transit: San Diego Trolley (Green or Blue line) to Santa Fe Depot, followed by a 5-minute waterfront walk.
driving: Paid public parking on Navy Pier adjacent to the ship.

name: La Jolla Cove
description: A picturesque sheltered cove carved into sandstone cliffs within an ecological marine reserve, world-famous for basking California sea lions, clear snorkeling waters, and spectacular sunset views.
transit: MTS Bus route 30 to Silverado & Herschel in downtown La Jolla, then walk 5 minutes down to the coast.
driving: Coast Boulevard street parking and paid village lots in downtown La Jolla.

name: The Art Institute of Chicago
description: Guarded by its celebrated bronze lions on Michigan Avenue, this legendary museum houses one of the world’s greatest collections of Impressionist and Post-Impressionist masterpieces, along with American Gothic.
transit: CTA ‘L’ train to Adams/Wabash (Brown, Green, Orange, Pink, Purple) or Jackson (Blue, Red).
driving: Park at Millennium Garages (Grant Park North or Millennium Park Garage) directly beneath Michigan Ave.

name: Millennium Park & Jay Pritzker Pavilion
description: Downtown Chicago’s premier 24-acre lakefront park featuring Frank Gehry’s Jay Pritzker Pavilion, Crown Fountain, the serene Lurie Garden, and world-class free outdoor concerts throughout the summer.
transit: CTA trains to Washington/Wabash or Millennium Station on the Metra electric line.
driving: Underground Millennium Garages accessible from Columbus Drive and Michigan Avenue.

name: Navy Pier
description: A 3,300-foot landmark pier extending into Lake Michigan, featuring the towering Centennial Wheel, Chicago Shakespeare Theater, sightseeing boat cruises, lakefront dining, and summer fireworks.
transit: CTA bus routes 29, 65, 66, or 124 connect directly to Navy Pier terminal.
driving: Dedicated indoor parking garages on Navy Pier (East and West garages).
